title: KV sparse-fusion allocator and eviction-wave compaction strategy
creator: Lena Martinez
description:
Problem: On multi-tenant dedicated hosts we observe long-lived micro-fragmentation in the GPU KV cache. Small token entries (~32-128B) leave gaps that prevent contiguous allocations for new KV pages; over time this increases active memory footprint and forces earlier evictions that increase CPU/GPU work and the 95/99ms tails for token-generation workloads.

Goal: Implement a low-latency, GPU-friendly allocation strategy that reduces internal fragmentation for small KV entries and provides a background compaction mechanism that consolidates free space without impacting steady-state latency SLOs.

Proposal (high level): Introduce a two-part system: (1) Sparse-Fusion allocator: packs many small KV lines into fixed-size fusion buckets (e.g., 4KB, 16KB) with compact headers and per-bucket freelists; and (2) Eviction-Wave compactor: a cooperative, bandwidth-limited background sweep that performs in-GPU consolidation of partially filled fusion buckets by migrating live entries into denser buckets using tensorized memcpy kernels and reclaiming contiguous spans.

Why different from existing slab/coalescer approaches: instead of global defragmentation or heavyweight relocation, Sparse-Fusion avoids creating many tiny free slots in the first place and keeps bucket meta small and GPU-local. The Eviction-Wave does progressive, locality-aware consolidation that marches across memory regions in waves, avoiding spikes in tail latency and providing predictable bandwidth caps per GPU.

Key features and trade-offs:
- Bucket sizing policy: use adaptive bucket sizes tuned by workload (default 8KB) to balance header overhead vs internal waste; larger buckets reduce header overhead but increase copy work during compaction.
- Per-bucket occupancy thresholds: fast-path allocations for >64B entries; very large entries bypass fusion and use existing slab path.
- GPU-friendly consolidation: use CUDA cooperative memcpy (or vendor-optimized tensor copy kernels) to move entries between buckets in-place where possible to avoid host<->device traffic.
- Eviction-wave pacing: rate-limit compaction by GPU memory bandwidth and schedule during low-latency budget windows; allow admin override in Dedicated.
- Fallbacks: if hardware/driver lacks fast device-side copy primitives, fall back to host-mediated consolidation with stricter rate limits.

Telemetry and instrumentation: new metrics and traces are required to validate correctness and measure benefit:
- per-bucket occupancy histograms
- fragmentation ratio by region (free_bytes / active_bytes)
- compaction bandwidth and time spent in compaction vs request-serving
- correlation of compaction events with generation latency (p50/p95/p99)

Acceptance criteria:
- Reduce observed fragmentation metric by >=30% in medium-entropy workloads (conservative target) and >=50% in low-entropy synthetic traces.
- No more than 5% relative increase in p50; p95/p99 must not regress by more than 8% compared to baseline during canary.
- End-to-end memory footprint reduced by >=15% on representative Dedicated instance fleet for typical chat workloads.
- Automated unit+integration tests for allocator invariants and non-corrupt compaction paths.

Design artifacts and links:
- Design doc (draft): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/KV/Sparse-Fusion+Allocator+and+Eviction-Wave
- Microbench harness and prometheus dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv-frag/eviction-wave-experiments
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood/serving/pull/12345

Engineering notes:
- Implementation phases: Phase 1 (prototype in rust allocator layer, host-assisted compaction), Phase 2 (device-side memcpy kernels and paced eviction wave), Phase 3 (production rollout on Dedicated with canary and telemetry thresholds).
- Memory layout: fusion bucket header is 64B aligned and includes a small checksum, occupancy bitmap for fast scans, and a versioned epoch counter to avoid race conditions with concurrent lookups.
- Concurrency model: read-path uses lock-free lookups into bucket slots (atomic versions); write-path uses a bucket-level spin / small mutex only for fusion inserts to keep latency low. Compactor acquires ephemeral ownership for a bucket using epoch compare-and-swap to guarantee safe movement.
- Compatibility: works with existing KV LRU/clock eviction controller; eviction-wave can be configured to run only when global free memory dips below a threshold.

Security and correctness considerations:
- Ensure checksum & epoch scheme prevents stale reads during in-flight compactions.
- Add heavy fuzzing and long-run mem-check in CI to catch corner-case races.

Rollout plan:
- Nightly experiments on canary machines (cluster: kv-proto-canary), gated by fragmentation reduction and latency regression thresholds.
- Canary window: 72 hours with automated rollback on metric regressions.
- Gradual ramp to 10% then 50% of Dedicated fleet with further tuning.

Stakeholders: Storage/Runtime, Inference-Perf, SRE (Dedicated), Devtools (telemetry).

Notes on cost vs benefit: Sparse-Fusion adds a small per-bucket header overhead but recovers more memory overall and reduces eviction churn; the worst-case copy bandwidth can be significant - hence the eviction-wave pacing strategy that trades off immediate compaction for sustained background consolidation.

References to related work: lightweight packed allocators, buddy+fusion hybrid strategies; previous internal experiments where host-side micro-defragmentation improved footprint but increased CPU overhead (see ENG-314159 experiments).
acceptance_criteria: >=15% end-to-end footprint reduction on representative Dedicated instances
unit and integration tests that validate allocator invariants
technical_notes: Prototype shows 18-35% reclaimed memory on low-entropy traces with bucket=8KB
Device-side memcpy reduces compaction time by ~3x vs host copy in microbenchmarks
Need careful tuning of bucket size by workload profile; include adaptive heuristic based on recent allocation histogram
risks: device-copy primitives unavailable on older drivers -> degrade to host-copy
mis-tuned bucket sizes could increase internal wasted bytes
compaction could compete for GPU bandwidth with inference if pacing misconfigured
